query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a nanohierarchical heterostructure into the CoCrFeNi matrix—by promoting the formation of nano-coupled grains and embedded nanoprecipitates—will enable adaptive friction interface protection that maintains low friction and wear from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a relatively homogeneous microstructure that suffers from elevated friction and wear at high temperatures due to rapid softening and inadequate tribo-oxidative protection
generation.intervention: Implement a thermal treatment or minor compositional modification that induces a controlled nanohierarchical structure featuring nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates homogenously dispersed in the matrix
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed over a temperature range from approximately 25 °C (room temperature) to 800 °C, under loads representative of tribological applications (e.g., around 5 N), and sliding speeds typical in laboratory reciprocating tests
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nano-coupled grains and well-dispersed nanoprecipitates
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, the nanostructure facilitates multiple deformation pathways that distribute frictional stress and reduce localized wear. At high temperatures, the same heterostructure enables a rapid tribo-oxidation response to develop a dense, nanocrystalline glaze layer that acts as a lubricious barrier against adhesive and oxidative wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the standard CoCrFeNi alloy, the engineered alloy should exhibit a reduced coefficient of friction and lower wear rates (potentially on the order of 10⁻⁷ to 10⁻⁶ mm³/Nm) consistently over the entire temperature range
generation.baseline: The original CoCrFeNi alloy without the engineered nanohierarchical structure, which shows increased friction and accelerated wear at higher temperatures due to its homogeneous microstructure
generation.boundary: Temperature from ~25 °C to 800 °C, a normal load around 5 N, and sliding conditions similar to those used in standard tribological tests (e.g., linear reciprocating motion), in an environment that does not exacerbate oxidation beyond what is typical in such tests
generation.uncertainty: While evidence supports adaptive heterostructures in other high-entropy alloys, the optimal processing conditions to reliably generate the desired nanoscale features in CoCrFeNi and the long-term stability of the protective glaze layer under cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses remain to be fully determined

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi samples: one set processed with the intervention to develop a nanohierarchical structure and one control set with the standard homogeneous microstructure. Conduct sliding wear tests across the temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under a constant load (∼5 N) and prescribed sliding conditions. Utilize real-time friction monitoring and post-test wear volume quantification along with microstructural analysis of the worn surfaces.
measurements: Surface microstructure (using SEM/TEM) to confirm presence or absence of a nanocrystalline glaze layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanohierarchical samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in both the friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range relative to the control, or if the expected adaptive glaze layer formation is not observed at high temperatures, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele
